
A launcher is a program that starts gitneighbr for someone, usually behind
its own local web address, alongside other tools. gitneighbr's **managed
mode** is made for this. Standalone use (`open_repo()`) is unchanged: it
keeps using your own Git, hooks, signing and credential helpers.

In managed mode gitneighbr:

- runs in the foreground with fixed arguments, and never opens a browser;
- serves its page and API under a path prefix, such as `/apps/gitneighbr/`;
- takes its session token from a header the launcher's proxy adds, so the
  page never holds a token and no token appears in any URL;
- runs a Git executable the launcher trusts, locked down so the repository
  can't make it start other programs;
- works only on the exact folder it is given;
- offers only the features the launcher enables, and refuses the rest on the
  server.

## Starting it

```sh
GN_TOKEN=... GN_SHUTDOWN=... \
Rscript --vanilla <library>/gitneighbr/scripts/serve.R \
  --repo=/path/to/folder --port=50123 --git=/path/to/git \
  --api-token-env=GN_TOKEN --shutdown-token-env=GN_SHUTDOWN \
  --base-path=/apps/gitneighbr/ \
  --features=local,remote \
  --git-config=/launcher/state/gitneighbr.gitconfig \
  --policy-file=/launcher/state/gitneighbr-policy.json
```

The same options are available from R as `gitneighbr_serve()`. Secrets are
passed by naming environment variables (`--*-token-env`), never on the
command line.

Once the socket is bound, one line is printed to standard output:

```
GITNEIGHBR_READY {"url":"http://127.0.0.1:50123/apps/gitneighbr/","host":"127.0.0.1","port":50123,"pid":4242,"version":"0.2.0"}
```

`GET <base>api/v1/health` needs no token. It reports `version`, `managed`, and
`busy` (a Git action is running).

To stop, send `POST <base>api/v1/shutdown` with both the session token and
the `X-Gitneighbr-Shutdown-Token` header. The reply is sent in full, any running
Git action finishes, and the process exits with status 0. The second token
matters because the proxy adds the session token to every request a page
makes, so the session token alone can't be enough to stop the server.

## The proxy contract

For every request under the prefix, the launcher's proxy must:

- forward the full path (prefix included), or strip the prefix (both work);
- set `Host` to `127.0.0.1:<port>`;
- add `X-Gitneighbr-Token: <token>`, and drop any copy the browser sent;
- drop `Origin`, `Cookie` and `Referer`, or pass a same-origin `Origin`.

gitneighbr checks every route except health: the `Host` must be the loopback
port, a browser-marked cross-site request (`Sec-Fetch-Site`) is refused, and
the token must match. So a page on another site can't use the child port
directly, even though it is on the same computer.

## Features

`--features=` is a comma list:

| Feature | What it offers |
|---|---|
| `local` (always) | status, changes, diffs, selected-file snapshots, `.gitignore` help, explicit setup, identity |
| `remote` | check destination, Send and Update with a full preview (below) |
| `tags`, `restore`, `trash`, `clone`, `github` | the standalone app's extra actions |

A route of a disabled feature returns `403 FEATURE_DISABLED` and does
nothing. Without `github`, nothing starts `gh` or calls the GitHub API, so
the page's regular status checks make no network requests.

## Git in managed mode

Git runs with:

- a minimal environment: no inherited `GIT_*` or `SSH_*` variables; the
  launcher can name more variables with `--pass-env`;
- no system or user configuration. `--git-config` is the only extra
  configuration file, and the identity form writes the name and email there;
- hooks, templates, fsmonitor, pagers, editors, signing, credential helpers
  and askpass all switched off;
- HTTPS as the only transport;
- `--no-ext-diff --no-textconv` on every diff.

The folder must be a Git working tree that starts exactly at `--repo`, or
not a repository at all (it can then be set up on request). Each of these
is shown with an explanation and can't be changed:

- a folder inside another repository;
- a `.git` file or link;
- `core.worktree`, alternates or submodules;
- a local setting outside a reviewed allow-list (for example
  `include.path`, filter drivers or credential settings);
- a `filter=` attribute (Git LFS, encryption).

## Policy file

`--policy-file` points to JSON written by the launcher, outside the folder:

```json
{
  "schema_version": 1,
  "groups": [{"id": "sources", "label": "Editable sources", "globs": ["recipe/**"]}],
  "default_group": {"id": "other", "label": "Other files"},
  "protected": ["runs/**"],
  "review": [{"id": "data", "label": "Study data", "message": "May identify people.", "globs": ["data/**"]}],
  "send_blocked": [],
  "ignore_template": [{"rule": "OUTPUTS/", "reason": "Rebuilt from a run."}],
  "max_diff_bytes": 200000
}
```

- **Groups** label changed files on the page. When a policy is set, nothing
  is pre-selected.
- **Protected** paths are never changed in the folder by restore, trash,
  ignore or Update.
- **Review** paths are marked on the page, and sending them needs an extra
  confirmation.
- **Send-blocked** paths make Send refuse.
- **Ignore template** rules are offered, one by one, only when the user
  explicitly sets up version history. They are written as a new
  `.gitignore`, and never over an existing one.

Globs are relative, use `/`, and support `*`, `?` and `**`. A trailing `/`
means everything under that folder.

## Send and Update

With the `remote` feature, nothing touches the network until the user asks:

1. **Check what would be sent** or **Check for updates** fetches only the
   destination branch.
2. The page then lists **every** snapshot that would leave or arrive. Each
   one shows every changed path with its size, and whether it is binary,
   marked for review, or blocked.
3. Send pushes exactly the listed commit. Update fast-forwards to exactly the
   listed commit. If anything changed in between, the action is refused.
   Diverged history, conflicts, protected paths and local changes to incoming
   files stop with an explanation. Nothing is forced, merged or rebased.

Only HTTPS addresses are accepted. The user enters an access token on the
page. It is kept in memory for the session and given to Git per command
through `GIT_CONFIG_*` environment variables, as an
`http.<address>.extraHeader`. It is never put on a command line, on disk, or
in any response.
